claim: JF-NP-26 is an inactive photocaged derivative of the metabotropic glutamate type 5 (mGlu5) receptor negative allosteric modulator raseglurant.
source: JF-NP-26 is an inactive photocaged derivative of the metabotropic glutamate type 5 (mGlu5) receptor negative allosteric modulator raseglurant.
evidence: The manuscript describes the chemical structure and design of JF-NP-26 as a photocaged compound based on raseglurant, supported by synthesis data and characterization.

claim: Violet light illumination of JF-NP-26 induces a photochemical reaction prompting the active-drug's release.
source: Violet light illumination of JF-NP-26 induces a photochemical reaction prompting the active-drug's release, which effectively controls mGlu5 receptor activity both in ectopic expressing systems and in striatal primary neurons.
evidence: Photochemical characterization data showing UV-visible absorption spectra changes upon 405 nm irradiation and quantum yield measurements support this claim.

claim: JF-NP-26 effectively controls mGlu5 receptor activity in ectopic expressing systems.
source: Violet light illumination of JF-NP-26 induces a photochemical reaction prompting the active-drug's release, which effectively controls mGlu5 receptor activity both in ectopic expressing systems and in striatal primary neurons.
evidence: Inositol phosphate accumulation assays and calcium imaging experiments in HEK-293T cells expressing mGlu5 receptors demonstrate light-dependent control of receptor activity.

claim: JF-NP-26 effectively controls mGlu5 receptor activity in striatal primary neurons.
source: Violet light illumination of JF-NP-26 induces a photochemical reaction prompting the active-drug's release, which effectively controls mGlu5 receptor activity both in ectopic expressing systems and in striatal primary neurons.
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments in cultured striatal neurons show light-dependent inhibition of mGlu5 receptor-mediated responses.

claim: Systemic administration of JF-NP-26 in mice followed by local LED-based illumination of the thalamus induces light-dependent analgesia in neuropathic pain models.
source: Systemic administration in mice followed by local light-emitting diode (LED)-based illumination, either of the thalamus or the peripheral tissues, induced JF-NP-26-mediated light-dependent analgesia both in neuropathic and in acute/tonic inflammatory pain models.
evidence: Chronic constriction injury (CCI) model data showing increased mechanical pain thresholds only after thalamic irradiation support this claim.

claim: Systemic administration of JF-NP-26 in mice followed by local LED-based illumination of peripheral tissues induces light-dependent analgesia in acute/tonic inflammatory pain models.
source: Systemic administration in mice followed by local light-emitting diode (LED)-based illumination, either of the thalamus or the peripheral tissues, induced JF-NP-26-mediated light-dependent analgesia both in neuropathic and in acute/tonic inflammatory pain models.
evidence: Formalin test data showing reduced nocifensive behavior after hind paw irradiation support this claim.

claim: Metabotropic glutamate (mGlu) receptors are widely distributed along the pain neuraxis and modulate pain transmission at different anatomical levels.
source: Metabotropic glutamate (mGlu) receptors are widely distributed along the pain neuraxis and modulate pain transmission (Kolber, 2015) at different anatomical levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kolber, 2015.

claim: Subtype-selective mGlu receptor ligands are considered as promising candidate drugs for the treatment of chronic pain.
source: Hence, subtype-selective mGlu receptor ligands are considered as promising candidate drugs for the treatment of chronic pain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field and supported by subsequent citations about specific ligands.

claim: Selective negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) of mGlu1 or mGlu5 receptors display analgesic activity in experimental animal models of chronic pain.
source: Accordingly, selective negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) of mGlu1 or mGlu5 receptors, and agonists or positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of mGlu2 or mGlu4 receptors have consistently been shown to display analgesic activity in experimental animal models of chronic pain (Montana and Gereau, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Montana and Gereau, 2011.

claim: Agonists or positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of mGlu2 or mGlu4 receptors display analgesic activity in experimental animal models of chronic pain.
source: Accordingly, selective negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) of mGlu1 or mGlu5 receptors, and agonists or positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of mGlu2 or mGlu4 receptors have consistently been shown to display analgesic activity in experimental animal models of chronic pain (Montana and Gereau, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Montana and Gereau, 2011.

claim: mGlu5 receptor NAMs (i.e. raseglurant) are under development for the treatment of neuropathic pain and migraine.
source: In particular, mGlu5 receptor NAMs (i.e. raseglurant) are under development for the treatment of neuropathic pain and migraine; however, their systemic use may be limited by mechanism-related adverse effects, such as hepatotoxicity, cognitive impairment and psychotomimetic effects (Friedmann et al., 1980; Gravius et al., 2005; Homayoun et al., 2004; Kinney et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about drug development status.

claim: Systemic use of mGlu5 receptor NAMs may be limited by mechanism-related adverse effects, such as hepatotoxicity, cognitive impairment and psychotomimetic effects.
source: In particular, mGlu5 receptor NAMs (i.e. raseglurant) are under development for the treatment of neuropathic pain and migraine; however, their systemic use may be limited by mechanism-related adverse effects, such as hepatotoxicity, cognitive impairment and psychotomimetic effects (Friedmann et al., 1980; Gravius et al., 2005; Homayoun et al., 2004; Kinney et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Friedmann et al., 1980; Gravius et al., 2005; Homayoun et al., 2004; Kinney et al., 2003.

claim: Alloswitch-1 is a selective photoswitchable mGlu5 receptor NAM that allows optical control of endogenous receptors.
source: We developed alloswitch-1, a selective photoswitchable mGlu5 receptor NAM, which allowed the optical control of endogenous receptors (Pittolo et al., 2014), in an attempt to achieve a light-dependent control of mGlu5 receptors within the pain neuraxis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pittolo et al., 2014.

claim: Alloswitch-1 shows mGlu5 NAM activity in its natural trans configuration in the dark, causing light-independent analgesic effects in animals.
source: However, alloswitch-1 and related photoswitchable compounds show mGlu5 NAM activity in its natural trans configuration in the dark, thereby causing light-independent analgesic effects in animals (Gómez-Santacana et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gómez-Santacana et al., 2017.

claim: JF-NP-26 was synthesized by modifying the aromatic amine group in raseglurant to generate a carbamate derivative of the violet-light absorbing coumarin DEACM in a one pot procedure.
source: Thus, we synthesized JF-NP-26 (Figure 1) by modifying the aromatic amine group in raseglurant to generate a carbamate derivative of the violet-light absorbing coumarin DEACM in a one pot procedure (Figure 1).
evidence: The synthesis procedure is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1, with detailed chemical methods provided.

claim: Transformation of the amino group of raseglurant into the coumarinyl carbamate shifted its main UV-vis absorption band from 338 nm to around 313 nm.
source: Transformation of the amino group of raseglurant into the coumarinyl carbamate shifted its main UV-vis absorption band from 338 nm to around 313 nm, and a second absorption peak appeared at 386 nm due to the coumarinyl phototrigger (Figure 2A).
evidence: UV-visible absorption spectra data in Figure 2A demonstrate this spectral shift.

claim: A second absorption peak appeared at 386 nm due to the coumarinyl phototrigger in JF-NP-26.
source: Transformation of the amino group of raseglurant into the coumarinyl carbamate shifted its main UV-vis absorption band from 338 nm to around 313 nm, and a second absorption peak appeared at 386 nm due to the coumarinyl phototrigger (Figure 2A).
evidence: UV-visible absorption spectra data in Figure 2A show this absorption peak.

claim: The UV-visible absorption spectrum of JF-NP-26 showed dramatic changes upon 405 nm irradiation, consistent with the photo-induced release of raseglurant and leaving the coumarinyl alcohol DEACM.
source: The UV-visible absorption spectrum of JF-NP-26 showed dramatic changes upon 405 nm irradiation (Figure 2C), consistent with the photo-induced release of raseglurant and leaving the coumarinyl alcohol DEACM (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the spectral changes upon irradiation, and the spectrum matches the sum of free raseglurant and DEACM spectra.

claim: The photouncaging quantum yield of JF-NP-26 was determined as φchem = 0.18.
source: The photouncaging quantum yield was determined by potassium ferrioxalate actinometry (Kuhn et al., 1989), as φchem = 0.18 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantum yield was measured experimentally using potassium ferrioxalate actinometry, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: JF-NP-26 didn't show NAM activity in dark conditions in the mGlu5-mediated IP accumulation assay.
source: Interestingly, while JF-NP-26 didn't show activity in dark conditions, its NAM activity was rescued upon 405 nm visible light illumination (pIC50 = 7.1; Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows dose-response curves demonstrating no inhibition in dark conditions.

claim: JF-NP-26's NAM activity was rescued upon 405 nm visible light illumination with pIC50 = 7.1 in the IP accumulation assay.
source: Interestingly, while JF-NP-26 didn't show activity in dark conditions, its NAM activity was rescued upon 405 nm visible light illumination (pIC50 = 7.1; Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows dose-response curves with calculated pIC50 value after illumination.

claim: JF-NP-26 was unable to restrain agonist-mediated signalling in dark conditions in calcium accumulation assays.
source: Interestingly, again while JF-NP-26 was unable to restrain agonist-mediated signalling in dark conditions, it abolished mGlu5 receptor-mediated intracellular calcium accumulation upon 405 nm irradiation (Figure 3C), thus demonstrating a light-dependent NAM activity.
evidence: Figure 3C shows quantification of receptor inhibition with no effect in dark conditions.

claim: JF-NP-26 abolished mGlu5 receptor-mediated intracellular calcium accumulation upon 405 nm irradiation.
source: Interestingly, again while JF-NP-26 was unable to restrain agonist-mediated signalling in dark conditions, it abolished mGlu5 receptor-mediated intracellular calcium accumulation upon 405 nm irradiation (Figure 3C), thus demonstrating a light-dependent NAM activity.
evidence: Figure 3C shows quantification demonstrating significant inhibition after 405 nm irradiation.

claim: Optical modulation of JF-NP-26 can be performed in a native receptor environment in cultured striatal neurons.
source: Results (Figure 3F) were comparable to those obtained in heterologous expression systems (Figure 3C), thus indicating that optical modulation of JF-NP-26 could also be performed in a native receptor environment.
evidence: Figure 3F shows calcium imaging results in primary striatal neurons comparable to HEK cell results.

claim: A single injection of raseglurant (10 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly increased pain thresholds in CCI mice regardless of light irradiation.
source: Interestingly, a single injection of raseglurant (10 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly increased pain thresholds in CCI mice regardless of light irradiation (Figure 4B; data with raseglurant after irradiation are not shown).
evidence: Figure 4B shows mechanical threshold data for raseglurant treatment in CCI mice.

claim: Systemic injection of JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly increased pain thresholds in CCI mice only after thalamic irradiation.
source: In contrast, systemic injection of JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly (p<0.01) increased pain thresholds in CCI mice only after thalamic irradiation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows mechanical threshold data demonstrating light-dependent analgesia with JF-NP-26.

claim: Formalin injection into the mouse hind paw induced an innate licking behavior that was significantly reduced by systemic administration of raseglurant (10 mg/kg, i.p.) in both phase I (70 ± 3%, p<0.001) and phase II (97 ± 1%, p<0.001) of the formalin test.
source: Formalin injection into the mouse hind paw induced an innate licking behavior that was significantly reduced by systemic administration of raseglurant (10 mg/kg, i.p., Figure 5, middle panel), thus demonstrating an antinociceptive efficacy both in phase I (70 ± 3%, p<0.001) and phase II (97 ± 1%, p<0.001) of the formalin test.
evidence: Figure 5 middle panel shows quantified antinociceptive effects of raseglurant in the formalin test.

claim: JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was unable to promote antinociception in dark conditions in the formalin test.
source: Noteworthy, while JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was unable to promote antinociception in dark conditions (Video 1), it elicited antinociception following direct hind paw irradiation both at phase I (54 ± 5%, p<0.001) and phase II (34 ± 5%, p<0.001) (Figure 5, middle panel; Video 2), demonstrating that JF-NP-26 was able to be peripherally photoactivated.
evidence: Figure 5 middle panel and Video 1 show lack of effect in dark conditions.

claim: JF-NP-26 elicited antinociception following direct hind paw irradiation both at phase I (54 ± 5%, p<0.001) and phase II (34 ± 5%, p<0.001) of the formalin test.
source: Noteworthy, while JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was unable to promote antinociception in dark conditions (Video 1), it elicited antinociception following direct hind paw irradiation both at phase I (54 ± 5%, p<0.001) and phase II (34 ± 5%, p<0.001) (Figure 5, middle panel; Video 2), demonstrating that JF-NP-26 was able to be peripherally photoactivated.
evidence: Figure 5 middle panel and Video 2 show quantified antinociceptive effects after peripheral irradiation.

claim: When the contralateral hind paw was irradiated, no antinociceptive effect was observed with JF-NP-26.
source: Interestingly, under the same experimental conditions when the contralateral hind paw was irradiated no antinociceptive effect was observed (Figure 5, middle panel, column C), thus demonstrating that a non-site specific peripheral photoconversion of JF-NP-26 does not yield systemic raseglurant-mediated analgesia.
evidence: Figure 5 middle panel column C shows lack of effect with contralateral irradiation.

claim: JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was able to cause substantial analgesia both in phase I (45 ± 9%, p<0.01) and phase II (90 ± 4%, p<0.001) of the formalin test in response to thalamic irradiation.
source: While JF-NP-26 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was inactive under basal conditions, it was able to cause substantial analgesia both in phase I (45 ± 9%, p<0.01) and phase II (90 ± 4%, p<0.001) of the formalin test in response to thalamic irradiation (Figure 5, lower panel).
evidence: Figure 5 lower panel shows quantified antinociceptive effects after thalamic irradiation.

claim: When the striatum was irradiated, no antinociceptive effect was observed with JF-NP-26.
source: Importantly, under the same experimental conditions when the striatum was irradiated no antinociceptive effect was observed (Figure 5, lower panel, column S), indicating that a CNS region of the pain neuraxis must be specifically irradiated to obtain pain control by JF-NP-26.
evidence: Figure 5 lower panel column S shows lack of effect with striatal irradiation.

claim: Uncaging of JF-NP-26 in the thalamus produced a stronger analgesic effect in phase II of the formalin test, which reflects mechanisms of central sensitization.
source: Significantlly, uncaging of JF-NP-26 in the thalamus produced a stronger analgesic effect in phase II of the formalin test, which reflects mechanisms of central sensitization.
evidence: Comparison of phase I and phase II effects in Figure 5 lower panel shows greater efficacy in phase II.

claim: The thalamic irradiation effects of JF-NP-26 were obtained after intraperitoneal administration, demonstrating its effective brain penetration in mice.
source: Finally, the thalamic irradiation effects of JF-NP-26 were obtained after intraperitoneal administration, demonstrating its effective brain penetration in mice.
evidence: The successful thalamic photoactivation after systemic i.p. administration implies brain penetration.

claim: A 3-day raseglurant treatment (50 mg/kg, ip) did not alter ALT and AST serum levels in mice.
source: Interestingly, while a 3-day acetaminophen treatment (300 mg/kg, ip) induced a significant increase in serum ALT and AST (Figure 6A), as described (Zhang et al., 2015), the 3-day raseglurant and JF-NP-26 treatment (50 mg/kg, ip) did not alter ALT and AST serum levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: Figure 6A shows serum transaminase levels after raseglurant treatment compared to vehicle and acetaminophen controls.

claim: A 3-day JF-NP-26 treatment (50 mg/kg, ip) did not alter ALT and AST serum levels in mice.
source: Interestingly, while a 3-day acetaminophen treatment (300 mg/kg, ip) induced a significant increase in serum ALT and AST (Figure 6A), as described (Zhang et al., 2015), the 3-day raseglurant and JF-NP-26 treatment (50 mg/kg, ip) did not alter ALT and AST serum levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: Figure 6A shows serum transaminase levels after JF-NP-26 treatment compared to vehicle and acetaminophen controls.

claim: A 3-day acetaminophen treatment (300 mg/kg, ip) induced a significant increase in serum ALT and AST in mice.
source: Interestingly, while a 3-day acetaminophen treatment (300 mg/kg, ip) induced a significant increase in serum ALT and AST (Figure 6A), as described (Zhang et al., 2015), the 3-day raseglurant and JF-NP-26 treatment (50 mg/kg, ip) did not alter ALT and AST serum levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: Figure 6A shows elevated serum transaminase levels after acetaminophen treatment, consistent with Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Raseglurant impaired novel object recognition at the dose of 20 mg/kg in mice.
source: Interestingly, raseglurant impaired novel object recognition at the dose of 20 mg/kg (Figure 6B), although it was inactive at 10 mg/kg (not shown).
evidence: Figure 6B shows that mice treated with 20 mg/kg raseglurant did not show preference for the novel object.

claim: Raseglurant was inactive in the novel object recognition test at 10 mg/kg.
source: Interestingly, raseglurant impaired novel object recognition at the dose of 20 mg/kg (Figure 6B), although it was inactive at 10 mg/kg (not shown).
evidence: The text states this explicitly, though data are not shown.

claim: Optic fiber implanted mice treated with vehicle or JF-NP-26 (10 or 20 mg/kg) and irradiated bilaterally at the ventrobasal thalamus showed a normal performance in the novel object recognition test.
source: Optic fiber implanted mice treated with vehicle or JF-NP-26 (10 or 20 mg/kg) and irradiated bilaterally at the ventrobasal thalamus (see above) showed a normal performance in the novel object recognition test (Figure 6A).
evidence: Figure 6B shows that JF-NP-26 treated mice with thalamic irradiation maintained preference for the novel object.

claim: Neither the systemic administration nor the thalamic photoactivation of JF-NP-26 cause memory impairment in mice.
source: Overall, these results demonstrated that neither the systemic administration nor the thalamic photoactivation of JF-NP-26 cause memory impairment in mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the novel object recognition test results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: JF-NP-26 is the first caged mGlu5 receptor NAM that has been shown to induce light-dependent analgesia in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain in freely behaving animals.
source: To our knowledge, JF-NP-26 is the first caged mGlu5 receptor NAM that has been shown to induce light-dependent analgesia in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain in freely behaving animals.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Raseglurant is a mGlu5 receptor NAM that has been shown to possess efficacy on the treatment of migraine.
source: Raseglurant is a mGlu5 receptor NAM that has been shown to possess efficacy on the treatment of migraine (Keywood and Wakefield, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keywood and Wakefield, 2008.

claim: The clinical development of raseglurant was discontinued because of liver toxicity.
source: However, its clinical development was discontinued because of liver toxicity (Marin and Goadsby, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marin and Goadsby, 2010.

claim: Light within the visible spectrum has a good tissue penetration and causes less tissue damage with respect to UV light.
source: This is highly advantageous for translational research because light within the visible spectrum has a good tissue penetration and causes less tissue damage with respect to UV light (Regan and Parrish, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Regan and Parrish, 1993.

claim: mGlu5 receptors are expressed in peripheral nociceptors, where they contribute to mechanisms of nociceptive sensitization by enhancing the activity of TRPV1 channels.
source: In fact, mGlu5 receptors are expressed in peripheral nociceptors, where they contribute to mechanisms of nociceptive sensitization by enhancing the activity of TRPV1 channels through a complex mechanism mediated by inositol phospholipid hydrolysis, prostaglandin formation, and protein kinase A-dependent phosphorylation of TRPV1 (Bhave et al., 2001; Karim et al., 2001; Neugebauer, 2001; Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Bhave et al., 2001; Karim et al., 2001; Neugebauer, 2001; Hu et al., 2002.

claim: The enhancement of TRPV1 channel activity by mGlu5 receptors is mediated through a complex mechanism involving inositol phospholipid hydrolysis, prostaglandin formation, and protein kinase A-dependent phosphorylation of TRPV1.
source: In fact, mGlu5 receptors are expressed in peripheral nociceptors, where they contribute to mechanisms of nociceptive sensitization by enhancing the activity of TRPV1 channels through a complex mechanism mediated by inositol phospholipid hydrolysis, prostaglandin formation, and protein kinase A-dependent phosphorylation of TRPV1 (Bhave et al., 2001; Karim et al., 2001; Neugebauer, 2001; Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Bhave et al., 2001; Karim et al., 2001; Neugebauer, 2001; Hu et al., 2002.

claim: The first phase of the formalin test reflects the activation of peripheral nociceptors.
source: In line with this, intraplantar JF-NP-26 uncaging showed higher antinociceptive efficacy in the first phase of the formalin test, which reflects the activation of peripheral nociceptors (Hunskaar and Hole, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hunskaar and Hole, 1987.

claim: The ventrobasal thalamus is the main relay station of the ascending pain pathway modulating the sensory, cognitive, and emotional components of pain.
source: Accordingly, mice were systemically injected with JF-NP-26, and fast antinociceptive effects were produced by light irradiation in the ventrobasal thalamus, the main relay station of the ascending pain pathway modulating the sensory, cognitive, and emotional components of pain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about thalamic function in pain processing.

claim: The second phase of the formalin test reflects the development of central sensitization to inflammatory pain.
source: Light-mediated delivery of raseglurant in the thalamus showed a greater antinociceptive efficacy during the second phase of the formalin test, which reflects the development of central sensitization to inflammatory pain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the formalin test phases.

claim: Neuropathic pain is characterized by a robust and long-lasting nociceptive sensitization that reflects a maladaptive process of activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: Neuropathic pain is characterized by a robust and long-lasting nociceptive sensitization that reflects a maladaptive process of activity-dependent synaptic plasticity (Basbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Basbaum et al., 2009.

claim: mGlu5 receptors participate in the expression of pathological synaptic plasticity at different levels of the pain neuraxis, from the spinal cord to the regions of the pain matrix including the amygdala and cerebral cortex.
source: Interestingly, mGlu5 receptors participate on the expression of this pathological form of synaptic plasticity at different levels of the pain neuraxis, from the spinal cord to the regions of the pain matrix including the amygdala and cerebral cortex (Neugebauer et al., 2003; Li and Neugebauer, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Hu and Gereau, 2011; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Neugebauer et al., 2003; Li and Neugebauer, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Hu and Gereau, 2011; Lin et al., 2015.

claim: Thalamic mGlu5 receptors are critical for the expression of nociceptive sensitization and can be specifically targeted by analgesic drugs in the treatment of neuropathic pain.
source: Our data indicate that thalamic mGlu5 receptors are critical for the expression of nociceptive sensitization and can be specifically targeted by analgesic drugs in the treatment of neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing analgesic effects after thalamic photoactivation of JF-NP-26.

claim: 405 nm light is safer than UV radiation for in vivo biological experiments.
source: Subsequently, we assessed the photochemical behaviour of JF-NP-26 upon exposure to 405 nm light (Figure 2B), which is safer than UV radiation for our in vivo biological experiments.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about light safety and tissue damage.

claim: The photolysis of the benzylic bond in JF-NP-26 generates a carbamic acid derivative that spontaneously decarboxylates to give raseglurant.
source: This process is likely involving the photolysis of the benzylic bond in JF-NP-26, thus generating a carbamic acid derivative that spontaneously decarboxylates to give raseglurant.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the observed photochemical behavior and known chemistry of carbamates.

claim: Systemic administration of inactive drugs that are activated by light on demand may provide a powerful strategy to reach a rapid control of pain limiting the development of dose- and mechanism-related adverse effects.
source: In conclusion, systemic administration of inactive drugs that are activated by light on demand may provide a powerful strategy to reach a rapid control of pain limiting the development of dose- and mechanism-related adverse effects that are typically encountered with conventional analgesic drugs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results demonstrating light-dependent analgesia without memory impairment.

claim: mGlu5 receptor NAM uncaging may be a suitable therapeutic approach for the local control of pain.
source: Our positive results constitute a proof of principle that mGlu5 receptor NAM uncaging may be a suitable therapeutic approach for the local control of pain, which could be applied in general to conditions of severe pain that are difficult to treat, and, in particular, to conditions of fast-onset severe pain that requires a rapid and highly localized treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful demonstration of light-dependent analgesia in multiple pain models.

claim: The transition from pre- to clinical settings still has to solve a number of practical problems, including assessment of photoactive compound stability and toxicity, as well as the development of implantable and remotely controlled LEDs.
source: However, the transition from pre- to clinical settings still has to solve a number of practical problems, including assessment of photoactive compound stability and toxicity, as well as the development of implantable and remotely controlled LEDs covering the photochemical needs to release the active compounds with light.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future challenges for clinical translation.

claim: mGlu5 receptors located at peripheral nociceptors and ventrobasal thalamic nuclei contribute differentially to acute inflammatory pain and mechanisms of central sensitization.
source: Hence, our data suggested that mGlu5 receptors located at two different stations of the pain neuraxis (i.e., peripheral nociceptors and ventrobasal thalamic nuclei) might be contributing differentially to acute inflammatory pain and mechanisms of central sensitization
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential efficacy of peripheral vs. thalamic photoactivation in phase I vs. phase II of the formalin test.

claim: A CNS region of the pain neuraxis must be specifically irradiated to obtain pain control by JF-NP-26.
source: Importantly, under the same experimental conditions when the striatum was irradiated no antinociceptive effect was observed (Figure 5, lower panel, column S), indicating that a CNS region of the pain neuraxis must be specifically irradiated to obtain pain control by JF-NP-26.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of effect when non-pain-related brain regions (striatum) were irradiated.

claim: A non-site specific peripheral photoconversion of JF-NP-26 does not yield systemic raseglurant-mediated analgesia.
source: Interestingly, under the same experimental conditions when the contralateral hind paw was irradiated no antinociceptive effect was observed (Figure 5, middle panel, column C), thus demonstrating that a non-site specific peripheral photoconversion of JF-NP-26 does not yield systemic raseglurant-mediated analgesia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of effect when the contralateral paw was irradiated.

claim: Raseglurant released from JF-NP-26 in response to light irradiation in the hind paw may interact with mGlu5 receptors present in peripheral nociceptors, thereby causing analgesia in the formalin test.
source: Thus, raseglurant released from JF-NP-26 in response to light irradiation in the hind paw may interact with mGlu5 receptors present in peripheral nociceptors, thereby causing analgesia in the formalin test.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed peripheral photoactivation effects.

claim: The ability to resolve analgesia with a fine resolution in time and space confers to the experimental approach a high significance for further development of new caged drugs acting at different levels of the pain neuraxis.
source: The ability to resolve analgesia with a fine resolution in time and space confers to our experimental approach a high significance for further development of new caged drugs acting at different levels of the pain neuraxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the work.

claim: Localized light targeting of peripheral and thalamic mGlu5 receptors represents a valuable strategy for the treatment of pain diseases.
source: Overall, upon local and thalamic photoactivation, JF-NP-26 demonstrated analgesic effects in two different models of pain, thus raising the interesting possibility that localized light targeting of peripheral and thalamic mGlu5 receptors represent a valuable strategy for the treatment of pain diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful demonstration of analgesia in multiple pain models and anatomical sites.

claim: The formalin test displays a first phase of pain (5 min after formalin injection in the hind paw), which models acute inflammatory pain.
source: The formalin test, which allows an objective analysis of pain based on nocifensive behavior, displays a first phase of pain (5 min after formalin injection in the hind paw), which models acute inflammatory pain, and a second phase (20–30 min after formalin injection), which models chronic inflammatory pain and reflects the development of central sensitization (Mogil, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mogil, 2009.

claim: The formalin test displays a second phase (20–30 min after formalin injection), which models chronic inflammatory pain and reflects the development of central sensitization.
source: The formalin test, which allows an objective analysis of pain based on nocifensive behavior, displays a first phase of pain (5 min after formalin injection in the hind paw), which models acute inflammatory pain, and a second phase (20–30 min after formalin injection), which models chronic inflammatory pain and reflects the development of central sensitization (Mogil, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mogil, 2009.

claim: Systemic administration of MPEP, a mGlu5 receptor NAM, reduced reference memory in rats.
source: For instance, systemic administration of MPEP, a mGlu5 receptor NAM, reduced reference memory in rats (Christoffersen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Christoffersen et al., 2008.

claim: Raseglurant had good clinical efficacy, tolerability and safety in a 2-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial.
source: However, despite good clinical efficacy, tolerability and safety in a 2-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (Zerbib et al., 2011), the long-term administration of raseglurant in migraine patients resulted in a disappointing high incidence of hepatic transaminase abnormalities, thus halting any further clinical development (Marin and Goadsby, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zerbib et al., 2011.

claim: Long-term administration of raseglurant in migraine patients resulted in a high incidence of hepatic transaminase abnormalities.
source: However, despite good clinical efficacy, tolerability and safety in a 2-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (Zerbib et al., 2011), the long-term administration of raseglurant in migraine patients resulted in a disappointing high incidence of hepatic transaminase abnormalities, thus halting any further clinical development (Marin and Goadsby, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marin and Goadsby, 2010.
